title: Learning from the Electronic Structure of Molecules across the Periodic Table
claim: A shared equivariant backbone encodes atoms and interactions, feeding separate heads that predict total energy and the full Hamiltonian matrix.
layout: 3 regions, left-to-right, backbone feeding energy head (bottom) and Hamiltonian head (right)
description: A dense architecture diagram split into three dashed or solid boxes. At lower left, a molecule icon with atoms A, B and C in teal, blue and yellow feeds upward into the Backbone box. The Backbone shows stacked translucent slabs for node embeddings and edge embeddings, with rows labelled l=0 to l_max and a channel axis C. Arrows lead through a dashed Node convolution and Edge convolution loop, repeated K times, to the output embeddings z_i^(K) and z_ij^(K). Below sits a small Energy Output Head: node convolution, a linear layer and the total energy E. On the right, the Hamiltonian Output Head has two rows, node and edge. Each uses a gate, an SO(3) linear layer, node parity expansion and tensor construction (TC). They produce a block Hamiltonian matrix H, with diagonal blocks in teal, blue and yellow and off-diagonal blocks in gray. The eye goes first to the colored slabs and then follows the arrows rightward.
caption: Architecture of HELM. Each rectangle in the backbone represents an embedding for an atom or inter-atomic interaction, has a shape of $(l_\mathrm{max}+1)^2 \times C$, and contains a set of learnable spherical harmonic coefficients for each $(l, m)$ up to a specified $l_{max}$. TC = Tensor construction layer to reconstruct the Hamiltonian (see [ref]).
abstract: Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) require vast amounts of atomic structure data to learn forces and energies, and their performance continues to improve with training set size. Meanwhile, the even greater quantities of accompanying data in the Hamiltonian matrix H behind these datasets has so far gone unused for this purpose. Here, we provide a recipe for integrating the orbital interaction data within H towards training pipelines for atomic-level properties. We first introduce HELM ("Hamiltonian-trained Electronic-structure Learning for Molecules"), a state-of-the-art Hamiltonian prediction model which bridges the gap between Hamiltonian prediction and universal MLIPs by scaling to H of structures with 100+ atoms, high elemental diversity, and large basis sets including diffuse functions. To accompany HELM, we release a curated Hamiltonian matrix dataset, 'OMol_CSH_58k', with unprecedented elemental diversity (58 elements), molecular size (up to 150 atoms), and basis set (def2-TZVPD). Finally, we introduce 'Hamiltonian pretraining' as a method to extract meaningful descriptors of atomic environments even from a limited number atomic structures, and repurpose this shared embedding space to improve performance on energy-prediction in low-data regimes. Our results highlight the use of electronic interactions as a rich and transferable data source for representing chemical space.
